question: BOSS pulled him off his own presentation to make him take notes instead. What pattern does this reflect?

options.text: Support work is assumed to be his regardless of what he'd earned or prepared
options.note: He spent half the night on it. That fact never enters the conversation, because the decision wasn't about the work.

options.text: "Sweetie" arrives before the instruction and does half of its work
options.note: It sets the register. By the time the actual sentence lands, the room already knows what kind of person is being addressed.

options.text: The reassignment goes to Linda without anyone weighing the two of them
options.note: Nobody compares preparation. Linda presents because Linda is the obvious person to present, and that obviousness is the whole problem.

options.text: A random scheduling mix-up with no deeper pattern
options.note: Possible on day two. It's the fourth time by Friday that this reading stops being available.

options.text: A performance issue with his previous work
options.note: He's two days in. There is no previous work, which is the point — the assessment arrived before any evidence could.

options.text: A rotation every employee goes through equally
options.note: Then it would have a name, a schedule and a next person. Track who takes minutes across the week.

question: He said "Actually, I'd really like to present. I've prepared extensively." What happened to that boundary?

options.text: It was brushed off with "cute" and overridden without consideration
options.note: "Cute" is the whole reply. It doesn't engage the request; it reclassifies the person making it.

options.text: He stated it correctly and clearly, and that changed nothing
options.note: Worth sitting with, because the advice he'll get later is to speak up. He did. On day two, plainly, with a reason.

options.text: The cost of asking landed on him — the room now has him filed as difficult
options.note: "We don't have all day" makes his one sentence the thing holding everyone up.

options.text: It was respected and he got to present after all
options.note: Linda presents. He takes notes.

options.text: It was discussed calmly and a compromise was reached
options.note: There was no discussion. Two words and an instruction.

options.text: He never actually stated it out loud
options.note: He did, on the record, in front of the room. Misremembering this is how "he never said anything" gets said later.

question: The room laughed at his "sonion rings" slip, and Linda was the one who pointed it out. What would ethical bystander behaviour have looked like?

options.text: Redirecting the moment rather than piling onto the laughter
options.note: Someone answering the actual lunch question would have ended it in four seconds.

options.text: Not repeating the slip back for a second, bigger laugh
options.note: The first laugh was reflex. Linda's callback was a choice, made after seeing the room go quiet.

options.text: Noticing that his suggestion was ignored before the slip was ever the subject
options.note: He was invisible first and funny second. The silence came before the laughter.

options.text: Waiting for him to laugh at himself first
options.note: That makes his own humiliation the permission slip, and he has to perform being fine to get it.

options.text: Recording it to raise in his performance review
options.note: Wildly disproportionate to a lunch order, and it moves a four-second problem into a formal process he'd have to survive.

options.text: Nothing — reacting to an honest mistake is fine
options.note: Reacting is fine. Repeating it for a bigger laugh, at the person the room had just ignored, is a different act.

question: He ends the scene thinking "just once I'd like to go a whole day without a bruh moment." What does that reveal, and what would help?

options.text: It's a pattern, not an incident — and naming the pattern helps more than excusing one moment
options.note: "Just once" is doing the work. He's counting, which means there's something to count.

options.text: He's already decided not to say anything about it
options.note: The thought is a joke he makes to himself. That's what it looks like when someone has worked out that raising it costs more than carrying it.

options.text: Asking what he'd want done, rather than deciding on his behalf
options.note: On day two he has no read on which of these people are safe. Handing him the choice is the only way he gets one.

options.text: He's overreacting to a single joke and should let it go
options.note: It isn't a single joke. It's the second thing in one meeting, and the meeting was his second day.

options.text: Nothing needs to happen — this is normal workplace banter
options.note: It is normal. Both things are true, and "normal" describes how often it happens rather than whether it costs anything.

options.text: He should be told to develop a thicker skin
options.note: This is the advice the game watches him take. By Friday you can see what it cost him.
